'''Flattenability''' in some <math>d</math>-dimensional [[normed vector space]] is a property of [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] which states that any [[Graph embedding|embedding]], or [[Graph drawing|drawing]], of the graph in some high dimension <math>d'</math> can be "flattened" down to live in <math>d</math>-dimensions, such that the distances between pairs of points connected by edges are preserved. A graph <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable if every [[Geometric constraint system#Types of systems|distance constraint system]] (DCS) with <math>G</math> as its constraint graph has a <math>d</math>-dimensional [[Geometric constraint system#Definitions|framework]]. Flattenability was first called realizability,<ref name="realizability">{{cite journal|last1=Belk|first1=Maria|last2=Connelly|first2=Robert|authorlink2=Robert Connelly|year=2007|title=Realizability of Graphs|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=37|issue=2|pages=125–137|doi=10.1007/s00454-006-1284-5|doi-access=free|s2cid=12755057}}</ref> but the name was changed to avoid confusion with a graph having ''some'' DCS with a <math>d</math>-dimensional framework.<ref name="flattenability">{{cite book|last1=Sitharam|first1=M.|last2=Willoughby|first2=J.|year=2014|chapter=On Flattenability of Graphs|title=Automated Deduction in Geometry|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=9201|pages=129–148|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-21362-0_9|isbn=978-3-319-21361-3|s2cid=23208}}</ref>

Flattenability has connections to [[structural rigidity]], [[Tensegrity|tensegrities]], [[Cayley configuration space]]s, and a variant of the [[graph realization problem]].

== Definitions ==
A distance constraint system <math>(G,\delta)</math>, where <math>G=(V,E)</math> is a graph and <math>\delta: E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{|E|}</math> is an assignment of distances onto the edges of <math>G</math>, is <math>d</math>-flattenable in some normed vector space <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> if there exists a framework of <math>(G,\delta)</math> in <math>d</math>-dimensions.

A graph <math>G=(V,E)</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> if every distance constraint system with <math>G</math> as its constraint graph is <math>d</math>-flattenable.

Flattenability can also be defined in terms of Cayley configuration spaces; see [[#Connection to Cayley configuration spaces|connection to Cayley configuration spaces]] below.

== Properties ==
'''Closure under subgraphs.''' Flattenability is closed under taking subgraphs.<ref name="realizability" /> To see this, observe that for some graph <math>G</math>, all possible embeddings of a subgraph <math>H</math> of <math>G</math> are contained in the set of all embeddings of <math>G</math>.

'''Minor-closed.''' Flattenability is a [[Graph minor#Minor-closed graph families|minor-closed]] property by a similar argument as above.<ref name="realizability" />

'''Flattening dimension.''' The flattening dimension of a flattenable graph <math>G</math> in some normed vector space is the lowest dimension <math>d</math> such that <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable. The flattening dimension of a graph is closely related to its gram dimension.<ref name="gramDimension">{{cite book|last1=Laurent|first1=Monique|authorlink1=Monique Laurent|last2=Varvitsiotis|first2=Antonios|year=2012|chapter=The Gram Dimension of a Graph|title=Combinatorial Optimization|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=7422|pages=356–367|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-32147-4_32|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-642-32146-7|s2cid=18567150}}</ref> The following is an upper-bound on the flattening dimension of an arbitrary graph under the <math>l_2</math>-norm.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="edgeBound">{{cite journal|last1=Barvinok|first1=A.|authorlink1=Alexander Barvinok|year=1995|title=Problems of distance geometry and convex properties of quadratic maps|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=13|issue=2|pages=189–202|doi=10.1007/BF02574037|doi-access=free|s2cid=20628306}}</ref> The flattening dimension of a graph <math>G = \left(V,E\right)</math> under the <math>l_2</math>-norm is at most <math>O \left( \sqrt{\left| E \right|} \right)</math>.

For a detailed treatment of this topic, see Chapter 11.2 of Deza & Laurent.<ref name="flatDimBound">{{cite book|last1=Deza|first1=Michel|authorlink1=Michel Deza|title=Geometry of Cuts and Metrics|last2=Laurent|first2=Monique|authorlink2=Monique Laurent|date=1997|publisher=Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-04295-9|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-540-61611-5}}</ref>

== Euclidean flattenability ==
This section concerns flattenability results in [[Euclidean space]], where distance is measured using the <math>l_2</math> norm, also called the [[Euclidean distance|Euclidean norm]].

=== 1-flattenable graphs ===
The following theorem is [[Mathematical folklore|folklore]] and shows that the only [[Graph minor#Minor-closed graph families|forbidden minor]] for 1-flattenability is the complete graph <math>K_3</math>.

'''Theorem.''' A graph is 1-flattenable if and only if it is a [[Tree (graph theory)#Forest|forest]].
[[File:1-flat.jpg|link=link=Special:FilePath/1-flat.jpg|thumb|440x440px|'''Figure 1.''' A 2-dimensional framework of a DCS whose graph is a tree with six vertices is shown in blue. A 1-dimensional framework of the same DCS is shown in red.]]
''Proof.'' A proof can be found in Belk & Connelly.<ref name="realizability" /> For one direction, a forest is a collection of trees, and any distance constraint system whose graph is a tree can be realized in 1-dimension. For the other direction, if a graph <math>G</math> is not a forest, then it has the complete graph <math>K_3</math> as a subgraph. Consider the DCS that assigns the distance 1 to the edges of the <math>K_4</math> subgraph and the distance 0 to all other edges. This DCS has a realization in 2-dimensions as the [[N-skeleton|1-skeleton]] of a triangle, but it has no realization in 1-dimension.

This proof allowed for distances on edges to be 0, but the argument holds even when this is not allowed. See Belk & Connelly<ref name="realizability" /> for a detailed explanation.
[[File:1 flat nonex.jpg|link=link=Special:FilePath/1 flat nonex.jpg|frame|'''Figure 2.''' For certain linkages, this graph has a 1-dimensional realization (e.g. the assignment of 1 to every edge). However, <math>C_3</math> can be obtained by contracting the edge <math>\bar{AB}</math>, so the graph is not 1-flattenable.]]

=== 2-flattenable graphs ===
The following theorem is [[Mathematical folklore|folklore]] and shows that the only forbidden minor for 2-flattenability is the complete graph <math>K_4</math>.

'''Theorem.''' A graph is 2-flattenable if and only if it is a [[Partial k-tree|partial 2-tree]].

''Proof.'' A proof can be found in Belk & Connelly.<ref name="realizability" /> For one direction, since flattenability is closed under taking subgraphs, it is sufficient to show that 2-trees are 2-flattenable. A 2-tree with <math>n</math> vertices can be constructed [[Recursion|recursively]] by taking a 2-tree with <math>n-1</math> vertices and connecting a new vertex to the vertices of an existing edge. The base case is the <math>K_3</math>. Proceed by induction on the number of vertices <math>n</math>. When <math>n=3</math>, consider any distance assignment <math>\delta</math> on the edges <math>K_3</math>. Note that if <math>\delta</math> does not obey the [[triangle inequality]], then this DCS does not have a realization in any dimension. Without loss of generality, place the first vertex <math>v_1</math> at the origin and the second vertex <math>v_2</math> along the x-axis such that <math>\delta_{12}</math> is satisfied. The third vertex <math>v_3</math> can be placed at an intersection of the circles with centers <math>v_1</math> and <math>v_2</math> and radii <math>\delta_{13}</math> and <math>\delta_{23}</math> respectively. This method of placement is called a [[Straightedge and compass construction|ruler and compass construction]]. Hence, <math>K_3</math> is 2-flattenable.

Now, assume a 2-tree with <math>k</math> vertices is 2-flattenable. By definition, a 2-tree with <math>k+1</math> vertices is a 2-tree with <math>k</math> vertices, say <math>T</math>, and an additional vertex <math>u</math> connected to the vertices of an existing edge in <math>T</math>. By the inductive hypothesis, <math>T</math> is 2-flattenable. Finally, by a similar ruler and compass construction argument as in the base case, <math>u</math> can be placed such that it lies in the plane. Thus, 2-trees are 2-flattenable by induction.

If a graph <math>G</math> is not a partial 2-tree, then it contains <math>K_4</math> as a minor. Assigning the distance of 1 to the edges of the <math>K_4</math> minor and the distance of 0 to all other edges yields a DCS with a realization in 3-dimensions as the 1-skeleton of a tetrahedra. However, this DCS has no realization in 2-dimensions: when attempting to place the fourth vertex using a ruler and compass construction, the three circles defined by the fourth vertex do not all intersect.

'''Example.''' Consider the graph in figure 2. Adding the edge <math>\bar{AC}</math> turns it into a 2-tree; hence, it is a partial 2-tree. Thus, it is 2-flattenable.

'''Example.''' The [[wheel graph]] <math>W_5</math> contains <math>K_4</math> as a minor. Thus, it is not 2-flattenable.

=== 3-flattenable graphs ===
The class of 3-flattenable graphs strictly contains the class of partial 3-trees.<ref name="realizability" /> More precisely, the forbidden minors for partial 3-trees are the complete graph <math>K_5</math>, the 1-skeleton of the octahedron <math>K_{2,2,2}</math>, <math>V_8</math>, and <math>C_5 \times C_2</math>, but <math>V_8</math>, and <math>C_5 \times C_2</math> are 3-flattenable.<ref name="realizability2">{{cite journal|last1=Belk|first1=Maria|year=2007|title=Realizability of Graphs in Three Dimensions|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=37|issue=2|pages=139–162|doi=10.1007/s00454-006-1285-4|doi-access=free|s2cid=20238879}}</ref> These graphs are shown in Figure 3. Furthermore, the following theorem from Belk & Connelly<ref name="realizability" /> shows that the only forbidden minors for 3-flattenability are <math>K_5</math> and <math>K_{2,2,2}</math>.
[[File:Partial 3-tree forb min.jpg|link=link=Special:FilePath/Partial 3-tree forb min.jpg|center|frame|'''Figure 3.''' The graphs of interest for 3-flattenability.]]
'''Theorem.''' <ref name="realizability" /> A graph is 3-flattenable if and only if it does not have <math>K_5</math> or <math>K_{2,2,2}</math> as a minor.

''Proof Idea:'' The proof given in Belk & Connelly<ref name="realizability" /> assumes that <math>V_8</math>, and <math>C_5 \times C_2</math> are 3-realizable. This is proven in the same article using mathematical tools from rigidity theory, specifically those concerning tensegrities. The complete graph <math>K_5</math> is not 3-flattenable, and the same argument that shows <math>K_4</math> is not 2-flattenable and <math>K_3</math> is not 1-flattenable works here: assigning the distance 1 to the edges of <math>K_5</math> yields a DCS with no realization in 3-dimensions. Figure 4 gives a visual proof that the graph <math>K_{2,2,2}</math> is not 3-flattenable. Vertices 1, 2, and 3 form a degenerate triangle. For the edges between vertices 1- 5, edges <math>(1,4)</math> and <math>(3,4)</math> are assigned the distance <math>\sqrt{2}</math> and all other edges are assigned the distance 1. Vertices 1- 5 have unique placements in 3-dimensions, up to congruence. Vertex 6 has 2 possible placements in 3-dimensions: 1 on each side of the plane <math>\Pi</math> defined by vertices 1, 2, and 4. Hence, the edge <math>(5,6)</math> has two distance values that can be realized in 3-dimensions. However, vertex 6 can revolve around the plane <math>\Pi</math> in 4-dimensions while satisfying all constraints, so the edge <math>(5,6)</math> has infinitely many distance values that can only be realized in 4-dimensions or higher. Thus, <math>K_{2,2,2}</math> is not 3-flattenable. The fact that these graphs are not 3-flattenable proves that any graph with either <math>K_5</math> or <math>K_{2,2,2}</math> as a minor is not 3-flattenable.
[[File:Octahedron embedding.gif|link=link=Special:FilePath/Octa.gif|thumb|330x330px|'''Figure 4.''' Construction steps to show the 1-skeleton of an octahedron is not 3-flattenable.<ref name="realizability" />]]
The other direction shows that if a graph <math>G</math> does not have <math>K_5</math> or <math>K_{2,2,2}</math> as a minor, then <math>G</math> can be constructed from partial 3-trees, <math>V_8</math>, and <math>C_5 \times C_2</math> via [[Clique-sum|1-sums]], 2-sums, and 3-sums. These graphs are all 3-flattenable and these operations preserve 3-flattenability, so <math>G</math> is 3-flattenable.

The techniques in this proof yield the following result from Belk & Connelly.<ref name="realizability" />

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="realizability" /> Every 3-realizable graph is a subgraph of a graph that can be obtained by a sequence of 1-sums, 2-sums, and 3-sums of the graphs <math>K_4</math>, <math>V_8</math>, and <math>C_5 \times C_2</math>.

'''Example.''' The previous theorem can be applied to show that the 1-skeleton of a cube is 3-flattenable. Start with the graph <math>K_4</math>, which is the 1-skeleton of a tetrahedron. On each face of the tetrahedron, perform a 3-sum with another <math>K_4</math> graph, i.e. glue two tetrahedra together on their faces. The resulting graph contains the cube as a subgraph and is 3-flattenable.

=== In higher dimensions ===
Giving a forbidden minor characterization of <math>d</math>-flattenable graphs, for dimension <math>d>3</math>, is an open problem. For any dimension <math>d</math>, <math>K_{d+2}</math> and the 1-skeleton of the <math>d</math>-dimensional analogue of an octahedron are forbidden minors for <math>d</math>-flattenability.<ref name="realizability" /> It is conjectured that the number of forbidden minors for <math>d</math>-flattenability grows asymptotically to the number of forbidden minors for partial <math>d</math>-trees, and there are over <math>75</math> forbidden minors for partial 4-trees.<ref name="realizability" />

An alternative characterization of <math>d</math>-flattenable graphs relates flattenability to Cayley configuration spaces.<ref name="flattenability" /><ref name="cayleyConfig">{{cite journal|last1=Sitharam|first1=Meera|last2=Gao|first2=Heping|year=2010|title=Characterizing Graphs with Convex and Connected Cayley Configuration Spaces|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=43|issue=3|pages=594–625|doi=10.1007/s00454-009-9160-8|doi-access=free|s2cid=35819450}}</ref> See the section on the [[#Connection to Cayley configuration spaces|connection to Cayley configuration spaces]].

=== Connection to the graph realization problem ===
Given a distance constraint system and a dimension <math>d</math>, the graph realization problem asks for a <math>d</math>-dimensional framework of the DCS, if one exists. There are algorithms to realize <math>d</math>-flattenable graphs in <math>d</math>-dimensions, for <math>d \leq 3</math>, that run in [[Time complexity#Polynomial time|polynomial time]] in the size of the graph. For <math>d=1</math>, realizing each tree in a forest in 1-dimension is trivial to accomplish in polynomial time. An algorithm for <math>d=2</math> is mentioned in Belk & Connelly.<ref name="realizability" /> For <math>d=3</math>, the algorithm in So & Ye<ref name="3_realizability_algo">{{cite book|last1=So|first1=Anthony Man-Cho|last2=Ye|first2=Yinyu|title=Proceedings of the seventeenth annual ACM-SIAM symposium on Discrete algorithm - SODA '06 |chapter=A semidefinite programming approach to tensegrity theory and realizability of graphs |authorlink2=Yinyu Ye|year=2006|pages=766–775|doi=10.1145/1109557.1109641|isbn=0898716055|s2cid=10134807}}</ref> obtains a framework <math>r</math> of a DCS using [[semidefinite programming]] techniques and then utilizes the "folding" method described in Belk<ref name="realizability2" /> to transform <math>r</math> into a 3-dimensional framework.

== Flattenability under ''p''-norms ==
This section concerns flattenability results for graphs under general [[Norm (mathematics)#p-norm|<math>p</math>-norms]], for <math>1 \leq p \leq \infty</math>.

=== Connection to algebraic geometry ===
Determining the flattenability of a graph under a general <math>p</math>-norm can be accomplished using methods in [[algebraic geometry]], as suggested in Belk & Connelly.<ref name="realizability" /> The question of whether a graph <math>G=(V,E)</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable is equivalent to determining if two [[Semialgebraic set|semi-algebraic sets]] are equal. One algorithm to compare two semi-algebraic sets takes <math>(4|E|)^{O\left(nd|V|^2\right)}</math> time.<ref name="basu2003algebraic">{{cite book|last1=Basu|first1=Saugata|title=Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry|last2=Pollack|first2=Richard|authorlink2=Richard M. Pollack|last3=Marie-Francoise|first3=Roy|authorlink3=Marie-Françoise Roy|publisher=Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg|year=2003|chapter=Existential Theory of the Reals|series=Algorithms and Computation in Mathematics|volume=10|doi=10.1007/3-540-33099-2_14|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-540-33098-1}}</ref>

=== Connection to Cayley configuration spaces ===
For general <math>l_p</math>-norms, there is a close relationship between flattenability and [[Cayley configuration space]]s.<ref name="flattenability" /><ref name="cayleyConfig" /> The following theorem and its corollary are found in Sitharam & Willoughby.<ref name="flattenability" />

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> A graph <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable if and only if for every subgraph <math>H=G \setminus F</math> of <math>G</math> resulting from removing a set of edges <math>F</math> from <math>G</math> and any <math>l^p_p</math>-distance vector <math>\delta_H</math> such that the DCS <math>(H,\delta_H)</math> has a realization, the <math>d</math>-dimensional Cayley configuration space of <math>(H,\delta_H)</math> over <math>F</math> is convex.

'''Corollary.''' A graph <math>G</math> is not <math>d</math>-flattenable if there exists some subgraph <math>H=G \setminus F</math> of <math>G</math> and some <math>l^p_p</math>-distance vector <math>\delta</math> such that the <math>d</math>-dimensional Cayley configuration space of <math>(H,\delta_H)</math> over <math>F</math> is not convex.

=== 2-Flattenability under the l<sub>1</sub> and l<sub>∞</sub> norms ===
The <math>l_1</math> and <math>l_{\infty}</math> norms are equivalent up to rotating axes in 2-dimensions,<ref name="flatDimBound" /> so 2-flattenability results for either norm hold for both. This section uses the <math>l_1</math>-norm. The complete graph <math>K_4</math> is 2-flattenable under the <math>l_1</math>-norm and <math>K_5</math> is 3-flattenable, but not 2-flattenable.<ref name="witsenhausen1986minimum">{{cite journal|last1=Witsenhausen|first1=Hans S.|year=1986|title=Minimum dimension embedding of finite metric spaces|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]|series=Series A|volume=42|issue=2|pages=184–199|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(86)90089-0|doi-access=}}</ref> These facts contribute to the following results on 2-flattenability under the <math>l_1</math>-norm found in Sitharam & Willoughby.<ref name="flattenability" />

'''Observation.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> The set of 2-flattenable graphs under the <math>l_1</math>-norm (and <math>l_{\infty}</math>-norm) strictly contains the set of 2-flattenable graphs under the <math>l_2</math>-norm.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> A 2-sum of 2-flattenable graphs is 2-flattenable if and only if at most one graph has a <math>K_4</math> minor.

The fact that <math>K_4</math> is 2-flattenable but <math>K_5</math> is not has implications on the forbidden minor characterization for 2-flattenable graphs under the <math>l_1</math>-norm. Specifically, the minors of <math>K_5</math> could be forbidden minors for 2-flattenability. The following results explore these possibilities and give the complete set of forbidden minors.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> The banana graph, or <math>K_5</math> with one edge removed, is not 2-flattenable.

'''Observation.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> The graph obtained by removing two edges that are incident to the same vertex from <math>K_5</math> is 2-flattenable.

'''Observation.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> Connected graphs on 5 vertices with 7 edges are 2-flattenable.

The only minor of <math>K_5</math> left is the wheel graph <math>W_5</math>, and the following result shows that this is one of the forbidden minors.

'''Theorem.''' <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fiorini|first1=Samuel|last2=Huynh|first2=Tony|last3=Joret|first3=Gwenaël|last4=Varvitsiotis|first4=Antonios|date=2017-01-01|title=The Excluded Minors for Isometric Realizability in the Plane|url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/16M1064775|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|volume=31|issue=1|pages=438–453|doi=10.1137/16M1064775|arxiv=1511.08054|hdl=10356/81454|s2cid=2579286|issn=0895-4801}}</ref> A graph is 2-flattenable under the <math>l_1</math>- or <math>l_{\infty}</math>-norm if and only if it does not have either of the following graphs as minors:

* the wheel graph <math>W_5</math> or
* the graph obtained by taking the 2-sum of two copies of <math>K_4</math> and removing the shared edge.

=== Connection to structural rigidity ===
This section relates flattenability to concepts in [[Structural rigidity|structural (combinatorial) rigidity theory]], such as the [[rigidity matroid]]. The following results concern the <math>l^p_p</math>-distance cone <math>\Phi_{n,l_p}</math>, i.e., the set of all <math>l^p_p</math>-distance vectors that can be realized as a configuration of <math>n</math> points in some dimension. A proof that this set is a cone can be found in Ball.<ref name="l1_lower_1">{{cite journal|last1=Ball|first1=Keith|authorlink1=Keith Martin Ball|year=1990|title=Isometric Embedding in lp-spaces|journal=[[European Journal of Combinatorics]]|volume=11|issue=4|pages=305–311|doi=10.1016/S0195-6698(13)80131-X|doi-access=free}}</ref> The <math>d</math>-stratum of this cone <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> are the vectors that can be realized as a configuration of <math>n</math> points in <math>d</math>-dimensions. The projection of <math>\Phi_{n,l_p}</math> or <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> onto the edges of a graph <math>G</math> is the set of <math>l^p_p</math> distance vectors that can be realized as the edge-lengths of some embedding of <math>G</math>.

A [[generic property]] of a graph <math>G</math> is one that almost all frameworks of distance constraint systems, whose graph is <math>G</math>, have. A framework of a DCS <math>(G,\delta)</math> under an <math>l_p</math>-norm is a generic framework (with respect to <math>d</math>-flattenability) if the following two conditions hold:

# there is an open neighborhood <math>\Omega</math> of <math>\delta</math> in the interior of the cone <math>\Phi_{n,l_p}</math>, and
# the framework is <math>d</math>-flattenable if and only if all frameworks in <math>\Omega</math> are <math>d</math>-flattenable.

Condition (1) ensures that the neighborhood <math>\Omega</math> has full rank. In other words, <math>\Omega</math> has dimension equal to the flattening dimension of the complete graph <math>K_n</math> under the <math>l_p</math>-norm. See Kitson<ref name="general_position">{{cite journal|last1=Kitson|first1=Derek|year=2015|title=Finite and Infinitesimal Rigidity with Polyhedral Norms|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|volume=54|issue=2|pages=390–411|doi=10.1007/s00454-015-9706-x|doi-access=free|s2cid=15520982|arxiv=1401.1336}}</ref> for a more detailed discussion of generic framework for <math>l_p</math>-norms. The following results are found in Sitharam & Willoughby.<ref name="flattenability" />

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> A graph <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable if and only if every generic framework of <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> <math>d</math>-flattenability is not a generic property of graphs, even for the <math>l_2</math>-norm.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> A generic <math>d</math>-flattenable framework of a graph <math>G</math> exists if and only if <math>G</math> is independent in the generic <math>d</math>-dimensional rigidity matroid.

'''Corollary.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> A graph <math>G</math> is <math>d</math>-flattenable only if <math>G</math> is independent in the <math>d</math>-dimensional rigidity matroid.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name="flattenability" /> For general <math>l_p</math>-norms, a graph <math>G</math> is

# independent in the generic <math>d</math>-dimensional rigidity matroid if and only if the projection of the <math>d</math>-stratum <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> onto the edges of <math>G</math> has dimension equal to the number of edges of <math>G</math>;
# maximally independent in the generic <math>d</math>-dimensional rigidity matroid if and only if projecting the <math>d</math>-stratum <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> onto the edges of <math>G</math> preserves its dimension and this dimension is equal to the number of edges of <math>G</math>;
# rigid in <math>d</math>-dimensions if and only if projecting the <math>d</math>-stratum <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> onto the edges of <math>G</math> preserves its dimension;
# not independent in the generic <math>d</math>-dimensional rigidity matroid if and only if the dimension of the projection of the <math>d</math>-stratum <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> onto the edges of <math>G</math> is strictly less than the minimum of the dimension of <math>\Phi^d_{n,l_p}</math> and the number of edges of <math>G</math>.
